perf.summary: The pointer hash `(int)(long)Value` discards the high 32 bits and the low ~3-4 alignment bits, clustering aligned allocations into few buckets; mix the full 64-bit value to a 32-bit hash to cut collisions.
perf.currentCost: GetHashCode returns the low 32 bits of the pointer. Heap allocations are typically 8/16-byte aligned, so the low 3-4 bits are constant, and contiguous allocations differ only in low bits — producing long open-addressing probe chains in any NativeHashSet<Ptr> (used by MemoryAllocator and previously by the pool), degrading Add/Contains/Remove toward O(n) under clustering.
perf.proposedChange: Mix the full 64-bit address, e.g. `ulong x = (ulong)Value; x ^= x >> 32; return unchecked((int)(x * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15UL >> 32));` (a fibonacci/xorshift finalizer), or at minimum `(int)((long)Value ^ ((long)Value >> 32))`. This spreads both halves and avoids alignment clustering.
perf.rationale: A well-mixed hash shortens probe chains in open-addressed Unity hash sets, directly speeding every Add/Contains/Remove that uses Ptr as a key. Low constant cost (a multiply + shift) for materially fewer cache-missing probes when the set is the data structure in play.
perf.risk: Behavior preserved: Equals is unchanged (still pointer identity), and GetHashCode only needs equal objects to hash equal — they still do. This becomes irrelevant if MemoryAllocator switches off the hash set (other ram opportunity) and the pool drops its set, so weigh against those; if any hash-set-of-Ptr remains, this is a clear win. Keep it unchecked to preserve wrap semantics.
